feedback: If you said 9.8 × 10⁴ > 3.2 × 10⁵ because 9.8 > 3.2, convert both: 98,000 vs 320,000 — the larger exponent wins, so compare exponents first and use A only to break ties.

If you ranked by coefficient alone — for example calling 9 × 10² the largest because its coefficient 9 is the biggest — remember 9 × 10² = 900 but 1.5 × 10³ = 1,500: a higher power of ten outweighs a larger coefficient.
Good: comparing exponents first and converting back as a check are two reliable ways to confirm your order.
activities.intendedInsight: For positive numbers in standard form with A normalised to 1 ≤ A < 10, the exponent dominates the comparison; the mantissa A only matters when exponents are equal.
learnerActions: Place 6.1 × 10⁵, 9.8 × 10⁴ and 2.3 × 10⁶ in order from smallest to largest; a magnitude scale strip can help you position them.
First decide the order by comparing exponents only (for these positive numbers, a bigger power means a bigger number), then use A only to break ties.
Test the trap directly: decide which is larger, 3.2 × 10⁵ or 9.8 × 10⁴; justify by exponent (5 beats 4) and confirm by converting to 320,000 vs 98,000.
Order 2 × 10³, 9 × 10² and 1.5 × 10³ and explain why 9 × 10² is smallest even though its coefficient 9 is the largest.
Write one sentence explaining your comparison method.
activities.title: Order standard-form numbers by scale

feedback: 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.00032, not 32000 — a negative exponent moves the decimal point left (the digits shift right into smaller place values).
47,000 = 4.7 × 10⁴ and 0.0032 = 3.2 × 10⁻³; if you got 4.7 × 10³ or 3.2 × 10⁻², recount by converting back.

If an answer fails its reverse-check, the error is often an off-by-one in the exponent, but it may be a wrong-direction shift (such as 32000 for 3.2 × 10⁻⁴) — recount the point moves and check their direction.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent two-way conversion, with a reverse-check habit, catches exponent miscounts and wrong-direction shifts.
learnerActions: Fill in the blank: 4,500,000 = ___ × 10ⁿ, keeping 1 ≤ A < 10 and stating n.
Convert 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ to an ordinary number, resisting the tempting wrong answer of 32000.
Convert 47,000 and 0.0032 into standard form, then convert each answer back to check you land on the original number.
For every answer, verify by reversing the conversion so an off-by-one exponent is caught immediately.
activities.title: Consolidate with two-way conversion checks

feedback: If you said 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ is negative, note that 10⁻⁴ = 1/10,000, a positive fraction, so 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.00032 > 0.
A convincing argument separates 'sign of the number' from 'sign of the exponent': the exponent only tells you how many times to multiply or divide by 10.
activities.intendedInsight: The sign of the exponent controls how large or small the number is, separately from whether the number itself is positive or negative.
learnerActions: Respond to the challenge: 'Is 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ a negative number? Convince me.'
Explain, using 10⁻³ = 1/10³, why a negative exponent produces a small positive amount, not a negative value.
Contrast 10³, 10⁰ and 10⁻³ on a place-value scale to show how the exponent's sign controls size but never the sign of the number.
activities.title: Argue about the negative exponent

feedback: Check that, in a base unit such as metres, very small quantities (atomic sizes) use negative exponents and very large ones (astronomical distances) use positive exponents.
A static scale illustrates purpose well but cannot perform or check your conversions — do the conversions yourself and verify them.
activities.intendedInsight: Standard form is a practical tool for expressing and comparing quantities that span many orders of magnitude.
learnerActions: Examine an orders-of-magnitude scale (for example from a grain of sand to a galaxy, or atomic size to astronomical distance) and express several labelled quantities in standard form.
For each quantity, state whether n is positive or negative and what that tells you about the size.
Explain why standard form is useful for writing very large and very small quantities compactly.
activities.title: Ground standard form in real scales
